segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again he went into a synagogue, and a man was there who had a withered hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were watching him closely to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to the man with the withered hand,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get up and stand in the middle.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to kill?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they were silent.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Looking around at them with anger, deeply grieved at the hardness of their hearts, he said to the man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Stretch out your hand.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees went out and at once began plotting with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great multitude from Galilee followed. And from Judea

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and from Jerusalem and from Idumea and beyond the Jordan and around Tyre and Sidon, a great multitude, hearing all that he was doing, came to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He told his disciples to keep a small boat ready for him because of the crowd, so that they would not crush him;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for he had healed many, so that all who had afflictions were pressing in on him to touch him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the unclean spirits, whenever they saw him, would fall down before him and cry out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are the Son of God!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he sternly warned them not to make him known.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he went up the mountain and called to him those whom he himself wanted, and they came to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He appointed twelve, so that they might be with him and so that he might send them out to proclaim

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to have authority to drive out the demons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He appointed the Twelve: Simon, to whom he gave the name Peter;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to them he gave the name Boanerges, which means Sons of Thunder);

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Cananaean,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and Judas Iscariot, who also handed him over.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat a meal.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When his family heard of it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He is out of his mind.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He has Beelzebul,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “By the ruler of the demons he drives out the demons.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he called them to him and spoke to them in parables:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How can Satan drive out Satan?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand; his end has come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But no one can enter the strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first ties up the strong man; then he will plunder his house.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, everything will be forgiven the sons of men—their sins and whatever blasphemies they utter;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness but is guilty of an eternal sin.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said this because they were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He has an unclean spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside, they sent word to him, calling him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A crowd was sitting around him, and they told him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, your mother and your brothers are outside, looking for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who are my mother and my brothers?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And looking around at those seated in a circle around him, he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Here are my mother and my brothers!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For whoever does the will of God, that one is my brother and sister and mother.”

notes.note: Supporters of the Herodian dynasty, here probably partisans of Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee. They are mentioned only in Mark and Matthew, and little else is known about them. The Pharisees were not natural allies of Herod’s house, so the alliance shows how serious the opposition had become.

Many early manuscripts add “whom he also named apostles” after “twelve,” and some editions print those words in brackets; they may have been copied in from Luke 6:13. The SBLGNT omits them, and this translation follows it. The repeated “He appointed the Twelve” in verse 16 is likewise missing from many manuscripts.

Mark transliterates a Semitic nickname and then translates it for his Greek-speaking readers. The first part reflects the word for “sons of,” but the exact Hebrew or Aramaic behind the second part is uncertain.

notes.traditional: Simon the Canaanite (KJV); Simon the Zealot (NIV, ESV)
notes.note: The byname has nothing to do with Canaan or Cana. It transliterates an Aramaic word meaning “zealous one,” which Luke 6:15 translates as “the Zealot.” Mark leaves it untranslated, and it is kept here as a name. Whether it points to personal zeal for the Law or to links with a militant movement is debated.

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing a person into someone else’s custody. The Gospels use the same word for what the priests and Pilate later do to Jesus. Most English versions say “betrayed” when Judas is the subject, and some scholars defend that as a legitimate contextual sense. “Handed over” lets the reader see the chain of handings-over that the Greek reader saw.
The Greek is literally “he comes into a house.” Without the article the phrase can mean “home,” probably the house in Capernaum mentioned in 2:1, or simply “into a house.”

notes.traditional: his friends (KJV); his family (NRSV, ESV, NIV)
notes.note: The Greek is literally “those from beside him,” an idiom that in this period usually meant a person’s relatives or household. Verse 31 suggests his mother and brothers are meant, though some take the phrase more broadly as his associates. “They were saying” can also be read impersonally, “people were saying,” in which case the family acts on a report and does not itself pass the judgment.

A name for the ruler of the demons, whom Jesus’ reply identifies with Satan. It probably goes back to a title of an old Canaanite deity (compare Baal-zebub in 2 Kings 1), though its exact meaning is disputed. The KJV’s “Beelzebub” follows the Latin tradition, not the Greek manuscripts.
A Semitic idiom for human beings in general, kept because the Greek preserves it. It is the plural of the phrase behind “Son of Man,” but here it is not a title.

Later manuscripts read “eternal judgment,” which lies behind the KJV’s “eternal damnation”; the earliest witnesses read “sin.” In Greek, “never” is literally “not into the age,” and “eternal” is the adjective formed from the same word, so the two halves of the verse echo each other.

Some manuscripts add “and your sisters,” and some editions print those words in brackets. The SBLGNT omits them. They may have been added in view of “sister” in verse 35, or dropped to match verses 31, 33 and 34.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts; “scribe” suggests a copyist to modern readers, and versions vary between “scribes,” “teachers of the law” and “experts in the Law.”
The exorcism sense recurs across the Synoptics and is rendered “cast out,” “drive out” or “expel”; it should be uniform so parallel passages match.
Very frequent across the New Testament; “preach” now suggests a sermon while “proclaim” reflects the herald’s announcement, and the choice should not vary by chapter.
Recurs in Sabbath and legal disputes and in Paul (“all things are permitted”); translators split between “lawful” and “permitted,” and parallel passages need to agree.
Used for the Lake of Galilee throughout Mark, Matthew and John; versions vary between “sea” and “lake,” and readers would be confused by inconsistency.

warnings: Verse 28: βλασφημέω is not rendered with a register form (slander; blaspheme; insult / hurl insults at / hurl insults) and has no register-exception note.
